sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events, E0–E2075. Attribution follows conversational context rather than ideological content. The transcript contains transcription errors and events spanning speaker changes; these mixed events are marked U. Audio was not supplied or consulted. No identifiable edited teaser replays occur in the retained transcript.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: if there is no immortality then all things are permitted
candidates.explanation: Craig endorses the quoted maxim while moving from death to moral irrelevance. E869–887 supplies a self-interest argument, but does not establish why unpunished wrongdoing lacks overriding reasons against it. Whether the maxim substitutes for that bridge or compresses an ordinary disputed argument remains uncertain; E945–947 expressly invites an alternative.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: ultimately it doesn't matter it all ends up the same
candidates.explanation: After Kagan distinguishes temporary significance from cosmic permanence, Craig repeats a compact conclusion without yet explaining why identical endpoints erase intervening value. However, E1326–1327 acknowledges harm, and E1350–1405 narrows the argument to accountability and conflicts with self-interest. Those qualifications leave slogan substitution uncertain rather than established.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: no genuine Christian would think like that
candidates.explanation: Kagan asks whether salvation permits wrongdoing without the personal consequences previously invoked to ground accountability (E1731–1740). Craig substitutes an authenticity exclusion for explaining that compatibility: anyone thinking this way falls outside genuine Christianity. E1717–1730 supplies repentance and transferred punishment, but the reply does not connect those qualifications to the challenged incentive argument.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: you're not morally obligated to do something just because it would be good for you to do it
contrasts.explanation: Craig supports the distinction between goodness and obligation with several worthwhile careers that one person cannot all pursue. The concise conclusion follows a concrete reason rather than replacing one.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.explanation: The emphatic phrase illustrates independence from popular opinion. Kagan supplies the harm rationale at E224–227 and explains categorical reasons at E234–255, with exceptions to the broader harm principle already acknowledged at E171–184. Its compact form does not establish substitution.
